questions.stemHtml: An elderly smoker had several episodes of hemoptysis in the past two weeks along with fatigue, headache, nausea, and anorexia. A chest radiograph shows an ill-defined hilar mass, and a transbronchial lung biopsy is performed. The microscopic appearance is shown. Which of the following laboratory test findings is most likely to be present in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Increased risk of cavitation

 

The microscopic image reveals keratin pearls, which are characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the lung. This form of lung cancer is strongly associated with smoking and frequently presents as a hilar mass on chest radiographs.

 

Squamous cell carcinoma often leads to central necrosis due to its location and growth patterns, which can result in cavitation within the lung. This is a common feature of squamous cell carcinoma, making increased risk of cavitation the most likely finding.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. High risk of thrombophlebitis: This is more commonly associated with adenocarcinoma, which has a higher incidence of causing hypercoagulable states and conditions like Trousseau's syndrome (migratory thrombophlebitis).

 

Option B. Presence of early metastasis: While lung cancers can metastasize early, small cell carcinoma is typically more aggressive and prone to early metastasis than squamous cell carcinoma.

 

Option D. Glandular differentiation: This would be indicative of adenocarcinoma, not squamous cell carcinoma. Adenocarcinoma tends to have glandular structures and mucin production, which are not features seen in this image.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is associated with keratin pearl formation, central necrosis, and an increased risk of cavitation. It is most commonly linked to a smoking history and typically presents as a hilar mass on imaging.

questions.stem: A child with skin rash, reduced platelet count, and high risk of infections should be evaluated for:

options.label: A
options.text: B cell tyrosine kinase activity detection

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) WASP gene mutation

 

The combination of skin rash, thrombocytopenia (reduced platelet count), and increased susceptibility to infections suggests a diagnosis of Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS). This is a rare, X-linked recessive immunodeficiency disorder caused by mutations in the WASP gene (Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome Protein).

 

WASP is characterized by the classic triad:

 

  1. Eczema (skin rash)
  2. Thrombocytopenia (low platelet count, leading to increased bleeding tendencies)
  3. Recurrent infections (due to immune deficiency)

 

WASP gene mutations lead to defective cytoskeletal reorganization in immune cells, impairing the function of both B and T cells, leading to immunodeficiency.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. B cell tyrosine kinase activity detection: This would be relevant for diagnosing X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton's disease), which typically presents with recurrent bacterial infections but does not involve thrombocytopenia or skin rash.

 

Option C. Adenosine deaminase activity: A deficiency in adenosine deaminase (ADA) is associated with severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), which leads to severe recurrent infections. However, SCID does not typically present with thrombocytopenia or skin rash.

 

Option D. CD40 defect on B cell: A CD40 defect causes Hyper-IgM syndrome, which leads to recurrent infections due to defective class switching in B cells. However, thrombocytopenia and skin rash are not characteristic of this condition.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome is caused by a WASP gene mutation and presents with the triad of eczema, thrombocytopenia, and recurrent infections, making B. WASP gene mutation the correct answer.

questions.stem: Hepatitis B is associated with an increased risk of liver cancer in patients because of:

options.label: A
options.text: Increased survival time in host cells

options.label: C
options.text: Enhanced release of tumor suppressor gene products

options.label: D
options.text: Integration of viral RNA with host DNA

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) High rate of hepatocyte proliferation

 

Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a DNA virus that leads to chronic liver inflammation and damage, contributing to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) development. The risk of liver cancer in patients with chronic Hepatitis B infection is due to the following reasons:

 

  • High rate of hepatocyte proliferation (B): Chronic HBV infection causes ongoing liver cell (hepatocyte) damage and regeneration. The increased hepatocyte turnover and proliferation increase the likelihood of accumulating genetic mutations, which can eventually lead to liver cancer.

 

Additionally, the HBV DNA can integrate into the host genome, which contributes to genetic instability and the inactivation of tumor suppressor genes, promoting oncogenesis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Increased survival time in host cells: While HBV can affect hepatocyte survival, this is not the primary mechanism contributing to liver cancer. The focus is more on increased hepatocyte proliferation and genetic mutations.

 

Option C. Enhanced release of tumor suppressor gene products: This is incorrect, as the virus can actually interfere with tumor suppressor genes, not enhance them. HBV does not enhance tumor suppressor function but may disrupt it, contributing to cancer development.

 

Option D. Integration of viral RNA with host DNA: HBV is a DNA virus, not an RNA virus. It integrates its DNA into the host genome, which can cause mutations and genetic instability. The presence of viral DNA, not RNA, is involved in the process.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Chronic Hepatitis B infection leads to increased hepatocyte proliferation due to continuous liver damage and regeneration. This process, combined with viral DNA integration, increases the likelihood of mutations and the development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

questions.stem: Due to which phenomenon do B cells express IgM and IgD antibodies at the same time?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Alternative RNA splicing

 

B cells express IgM and IgD simultaneously on their surface during early stages of development. This occurs due to alternative RNA splicing of the same heavy chain transcript. Both IgM and IgD share the same variable region for antigen specificity, but the constant region differs due to alternative splicing of the mRNA, allowing for the co-expression of these two isotypes.

 

Mechanism:

 

  • Both IgM and IgD heavy chain constant regions (Cμ and Cδ) are encoded in the same VDJ-rearranged transcript.
  • After successful VDJ recombination, the primary RNA transcript includes both Cμ and Cδ constant region exons.
  • Through alternative splicing, the B cell can produce:
  • IgM mRNA (Cμ)
  • IgD mRNA (Cδ)
  • This allows surface co-expression of IgM and IgD with the same antigen specificity.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Somatic hypermutation: This process occurs later, primarily in germinal centers, and introduces point mutations into the variable region of the antibody genes to increase affinity for the antigen. It does not explain the simultaneous expression of IgM and IgD.

 

Option C. Affinity maturation: This process involves the selection of B cells that produce antibodies with higher affinity for the antigen after somatic hypermutation. It does not play a role in the simultaneous expression of IgM and IgD.

 

Option D. Allelic exclusion: This process ensures that B cells express a single heavy chain and a single light chain allele, leading to the production of one type of antibody with a specific antigen-binding site. It ensures monospecificity of B cell receptors, but it is not related to the simultaneous expression of IgM and IgD.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The simultaneous expression of IgM and IgD on B cells is due to alternative RNA splicing of the heavy chain gene, allowing both isotypes to be produced from the same primary transcript.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male presents with severe flank pain that radiates to the groin. He describes the pain as sudden and excruciating. Laboratory tests reveal hematuria, and imaging shows a 5mm stone located at the ureteropelvic junction of the right kidney. The patient's urine pH is 7.6. Which of the following crystals may be seen in the urine of this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Coffin lid crystals

 

The patient's symptoms of severe flank pain radiating to the groin, hematuria, and the imaging finding of a stone at the ureteropelvic junction are classic signs of nephrolithiasis (kidney stone disease). The urine pH of 7.6 indicates alkaline urine, which is a key factor in determining the type of stone and associated crystal formation.

 

  • Coffin lid crystals (D) are characteristic of struvite stones (also known as magnesium ammonium phosphate stones). These stones typically form in alkaline urine and are associated with urease-producing bacteria, such as Proteus or Klebsiella, that raise urine pH. These crystals have a characteristic coffin lid appearance under microscopic examination.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Rosette shaped crystals: These crystals are typically associated with uric acid stones, which form in acidic urine (pH < 5.5), not in alkaline urine. Uric acid crystals are unlikely in this patient, given the high urine pH.

 

Option B. Hexagonal crystals: Hexagonal crystals are seen in patients with cystinuria, a genetic disorder that causes cystine stones. These stones also tend to form in acidic urine, making it less likely in this case.

 

Option C. Dumb-bell shaped crystals: Dumb-bell shaped crystals are characteristic of calcium oxalate stones, which can form in either acidic or neutral urine, but they are not strongly associated with alkaline urine or the elevated urine pH seen in this patient.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Coffin lid crystals are characteristic of struvite stones, which form in alkaline urine and are associated with urease-producing bacteria. This patient's urine pH of 7.6 makes struvite stones the most likely diagnosis.

questions.stem: Arrange the following steps of platelet changes in the correct sequence during hemostasis:

options.label: A
options.text: Platelet activation → Platelet adhesion → Platelet aggregation

options.label: B
options.text: Platelet activation → Platelet aggregation → Platelet adhesion

options.label: C
options.text: Platelet aggregation → Platelet activation → Platelet adhesion

options.label: D
options.text: Platelet adhesion → Platelet activation → Platelet aggregation

questions.answerText: Platelet adhesion → Platelet activation → Platelet aggregation
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Platelet adhesion → Platelet activation → Platelet aggregation

 

During hemostasis, platelets undergo several sequential changes to form a clot and stop bleeding. The correct sequence of events is as follows:

 

  1. Platelet adhesion:
    • Platelets adhere to the exposed subendothelial collagen at the site of vascular injury. This process is mediated by von Willebrand factor (vWF), which binds to the platelet surface receptor glycoprotein Ib (GpIb). This step is crucial for anchoring the platelets at the site of injury.
  2. Platelet activation:
    • Once adhered, platelets undergo activation, which involves changes in their shape and the release of chemical signals (e.g., ADP, thromboxane A2) that enhance further platelet recruitment. This activation step also exposes the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (GpIIb/IIIa) receptor on the platelet surface.
  3. Platelet aggregation:
    • Finally, platelets aggregate by linking together through fibrinogen bridges that bind to the activated GpIIb/IIIa receptors on adjacent platelets. This process leads to the formation of a platelet plug at the site of injury, effectively stopping the bleeding.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The correct sequence of events in platelet hemostasis is platelet adhesion → platelet activation → platelet aggregation. This process is essential for the formation of a stable platelet plug in response to vascular injury.

questions.stem: A pathologist is examining the liver biopsy of a 20-year-old male with cirrhosis. A Prussian blue stain reveals extensive positivity. Laboratory testing does not reveal HbH or Hb Barts. Of the following, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) β-thalassemia major

 

The Prussian blue stain is used to detect iron in tissues, and extensive positivity indicates iron overload. In a young patient with cirrhosis and iron overload, the most likely cause is a chronic hemolytic anemia requiring multiple blood transfusions, which leads to secondary iron overload. β-thalassemia major fits this scenario, where the patient has received frequent transfusions to manage severe anemia.

 

Key points supporting the diagnosis of β-thalassemia major:

 

  1. Cirrhosis: Iron overload from repeated blood transfusions in β-thalassemia major can lead to iron deposition in various organs, including the liver, resulting in cirrhosis.
  2. Prussian blue stain: Extensive positivity in the liver biopsy confirms significant iron accumulation, which is typical in conditions with chronic iron overload like β-thalassemia major.
  3. Absence of HbH or Hb Barts: These are typically seen in α-thalassemia (HbH with three α gene deletions and Hb Barts with four α gene deletions). Their absence points away from α-thalassemia and suggests a different diagnosis, such as β-thalassemia major.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. α-thalassemia: While HbH and Hb Barts are characteristic of α-thalassemia, their absence in this case makes this diagnosis unlikely. Furthermore, α-thalassemia typically presents with different clinical and hematological features.

 

Option C. Severe iron deficiency anemia: Iron deficiency anemia would result in low iron stores, not iron overload. A Prussian blue stain would likely show negative or minimal staining in this case.

 

Option D. β-thalassemia minor: This is the milder form of β-thalassemia and is unlikely to result in significant iron overload or cirrhosis. Patients with β-thalassemia minor generally do not require regular blood transfusions, so they do not develop the iron overload seen in this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The extensive iron deposition seen on the Prussian blue stain, in combination with the absence of HbH or Hb Barts and the history of cirrhosis, strongly suggests β-thalassemia major, where chronic transfusions lead to secondary iron overload.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old patient presents with a severe headache, tenderness over the temples, and vision changes, including sudden, painless, and complete loss of vision in one eye. Examination reveals temporal artery tenderness and a palpable, cord-like temporal artery. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Giant cell arteritis

 

This patient’s presentation is highly suggestive of giant cell arteritis (GCA), also known as temporal arteritis, a vasculitis affecting medium and large-sized arteries, particularly the temporal artery in elderly individuals. Several features of the case confirm this diagnosis:

 

  1. Elderly age (70 years old): GCA is most commonly seen in patients over the age of 50, typically around 70 years of age or older.
  2. Severe headache and temporal artery tenderness: The classic presentation of GCA includes a new, localized headache over the temporal area with tenderness and sometimes a palpable, cord-like temporal artery.
  3. Sudden painless loss of vision: GCA can cause ischemic optic neuropathy, leading to sudden, painless vision loss, which is a serious complication and requires immediate treatment to prevent permanent blindness.
  4. High ESR: An elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is a hallmark laboratory finding in GCA, typically above 50 mm/hr, often much higher. This reflects the inflammatory nature of the disease.
  5. Biopsy findings in GCA: A definitive diagnosis can be made with a temporal artery biopsy, which shows giant cells and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina, characteristic histological features of GCA. The biopsy is stained using the Von Gieson stain or Verhoeff’s elastic stain to highlight the internal elastic lamina, which is often fragmented in GCA.
  6. Polymyalgia Rheumatica: GCA is often associated with polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR), which presents with shoulder and pelvic girdle pain and stiffness. This is another important clinical clue supporting the diagnosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cluster headache: While cluster headaches cause severe, unilateral pain around the eye, they are typically episodic, occurring in younger individuals, and are not associated with vision loss or temporal artery tenderness.

 

Option B. Migraine with aura: Migraines can present with severe headaches and visual disturbances (like an aura), but they are not typically associated with the palpable temporal artery, vision loss, or elevated ESR, as seen in GCA.

 

Option D. Tension headache: Tension headaches cause mild to moderate generalized headaches and are not associated with focal symptoms such as temporal artery tenderness, vision loss, or systemic inflammation (e.g., high ESR).

 

Educational Objective:

 

Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is characterized by new-onset headaches, vision loss, temporal artery tenderness, and elevated ESR in elderly patients. A temporal artery biopsy showing fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina and giant cells, along with a positive Von Gieson stain or Verhoeff's elastic stain, confirms the diagnosis. Immediate treatment with corticosteroids is necessary to prevent permanent vision loss.

questions.stem: In the case of a fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of the thyroid, which of the following is a standard criterion for calling it an adequate sample?

options.label: A
options.text: At least 10 groups of minimum 6 follicular cells each

options.label: B
options.text: At least 6 groups of minimum 10 follicular cells each

options.label: C
options.text: At least 3 groups of minimum 10 follicular cells each

options.label: D
options.text: At least 10 groups of minimum 10 follicular cells each

questions.answerText: At least 6 groups of minimum 10 follicular cells each

Ans. B) At least 6 groups of minimum 10 follicular cells each

 

For a thyroid FNAC sample to be considered adequate, cytological criteria require the presence of at least 6 groups of follicular cells, with each group containing at least 10 cells. This is in accordance with the Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology, which sets guidelines for determining sample adequacy:

 

  1. Adequate sampling ensures there is enough cellular material for accurate evaluation and diagnosis of potential thyroid lesions.
  2. 6 groups of at least 10 follicular cells allow the cytopathologist to properly assess the cellular architecture and identify abnormalities, including neoplastic processes.
  3. Inadequate samples with fewer cells or groups may lead to an inconclusive diagnosis and require repeat FNAC.

The standard adequacy criterion for a thyroid FNAC sample is at least 6 groups of at least 10 follicular cells each.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about "liquid biopsy" in comparison to standard tissue biopsy?

options.label: B
options.text: Can be useful for detection of metastatic subclones of a malignant tumor

options.label: C
options.text: Amount of biological sample is greater in amount

questions.answerText: Amount of biological sample is greater in amount
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Amount of biological sample is greater in amount

 

A liquid biopsy is a non-invasive method of analyzing tumors through the collection of blood or other bodily fluids, such as plasma, to detect circulating tumor cells (CTCs) or cell-free tumor DNA (ctDNA). It is increasingly being used in cancer diagnostics and monitoring.

 

A liquid biopsy generally involves a smaller biological sample compared to traditional tissue biopsies. It captures only small amounts of circulating tumor cells or ctDNA, making the sample size smaller in comparison to the larger tissue sample obtained in a standard biopsy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Easier to perform (True): Liquid biopsies require only a blood sample, making them much easier to perform than traditional tissue biopsies, which may require surgical intervention or more invasive procedures.

 

Option B. Can be useful for detection of metastatic subclones of a malignant tumor (True): Liquid biopsies can detect circulating tumor DNA or cells from metastatic subclones that may not be captured by a tissue biopsy, offering insights into the tumor's heterogeneity and evolution.

 

Option D. Less invasive (True): Liquid biopsies are less invasive, requiring only a blood draw, whereas tissue biopsies involve more invasive techniques such as needle biopsies or surgical procedures.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The false statement is C. Amount of biological sample is greater in amount, as liquid biopsies require smaller biological samples compared to traditional tissue biopsies. This is one of the reasons liquid biopsies are easier and less invasive.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the "cell within cell" appearance is not correctly matched?

options.label: A
options.text: Emperipolesis: movement of live cells following internalization

options.label: B
options.text: Efferocytosis: capture and deletion of dying cells by efferocytosis

options.label: D

questions.answerText: Entosis: active internalization of a dead cell into another cell's cytoplasm
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Entosis: active internalization of a dead cell into another cell's cytoplasm

 

Entosis (False, Correct Answer):

 

  • Definition: Entosis involves the active internalization of a live cell, not a dead cell, into another cell's cytoplasm. The engulfed cell is often alive at the time of internalization, and it may eventually undergo degradation inside the host cell.
  • Example: This phenomenon is often observed in cancer, where one live epithelial cell invades another.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Emperipolesis (True):

 

  • Definition: The process in which a live cell (often a lymphocyte or neutrophil) moves through the cytoplasm of another cell without being degraded. This is a temporary phenomenon where the engulfed cell can exit without damage.
  • Example: Seen in megakaryocytes in bone marrow where live cells pass through.

 

Option B. Efferocytosis (True):

 

  • Definition: The process by which dying or apoptotic cells are recognized and engulfed by phagocytic cells (usually macrophages), ensuring their removal and deletion from the tissue. This is crucial for maintaining tissue homeostasis.
  • Example: Clearing of apoptotic cells during inflammation.

 

Option D. Enclysis (True):

 

  • Definition: Enclysis refers to the confinement of live cells, such as CD4+ T cells, within hepatocytes. This phenomenon has been observed in certain liver diseases.
  • Example: CD4+ T cells are engulfed but not degraded, remaining within the hepatocytes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The incorrectly matched pair is C. Entosis: active internalization of a dead cell into another cell's cytoplasm. Entosis involves the internalization of live cells, not dead cells.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with a painless breast lump. Clinical examination reveals a palpable, firm, non-tender mass, and a mammogram shows an irregular mass with spiculated margins and microcalcifications. A diagnosis of breast cancer is made. Which of the following is correct about the disease? Most common location is the upper outer quadrant of her left breast.Usually arises from terminal duct lobular unit.Nulliparity is protective.Molecular classification of breast cancer is based on gene expression profiling.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 1, 2, 4

 

Let's go through the statements one by one:

 

1. Most common location is the upper outer quadrant of her left breast: This is true. Breast cancer most frequently occurs in the upper outer quadrant of the breast because this area contains the most glandular tissue.

 

2. Usually arises from terminal duct lobular unit: This is true. The majority of breast cancers, including ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and invasive ductal carcinoma, arise from the terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU), which is the functional unit of the breast.

 

4. Molecular classification of breast cancer is based on gene expression profiling: This is true. Molecular classification divides breast cancer into subtypes based on gene expression profiling, such as luminal A, luminal B, HER2-positive, and triple-negative breast cancers. These classifications are important for determining prognosis and treatment strategies.

 

Other Options:

 

Option 3. Nulliparity is protective: This is false. Nulliparity (having never given birth) is a risk factor, not protective, for breast cancer. Women who have never been pregnant have a longer lifetime exposure to estrogen, which increases the risk of breast cancer.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Breast cancer most commonly occurs in the upper outer quadrant and arises from the terminal duct lobular unit. Nulliparity is a risk factor, not protective, and the molecular classification of breast cancer is based on gene expression profiling.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old patient presented with a rectal mass measuring 2.5 cm by 3 cm. On biopsy, it showed the presence of colonic mucosa with multiple dilated glands filled with mucin and inflammatory cells. Which of the following is a likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Hamartoma

 

The biopsy description showing colonic mucosa with multiple dilated glands filled with mucin and inflammatory cells is consistent with a juvenile polyp, which is a type of hamartoma. Juvenile polyps are the most common rectal polyps in children and are benign lesions composed of overgrowths of normal tissue, often with dilated glands and abundant mucin. These polyps can present as a rectal mass and may cause rectal bleeding.

 

A hamartoma is a benign, disorganized overgrowth of tissue that is normally found in the affected area. In this case, the presence of colonic mucosa with dilated glands and mucin is typical of a juvenile polyp, a type of hamartomatous lesion commonly found in the rectum of children.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Choristoma: A choristoma refers to the presence of normal tissue in an abnormal location (ectopic tissue). This diagnosis is unlikely here because the biopsy findings show normal colonic tissue in its normal location (the rectum), indicating that this is not a case of ectopic tissue.

 

Option C. Adenoma: Adenomas are benign neoplasms that arise from glandular tissue and have potential to progress to malignancy, particularly in adults. While adenomas can be found in the colon, the biopsy findings of dilated glands with mucin and inflammatory cells are more consistent with a juvenile polyp (hamartoma) rather than an adenoma, which typically has a dysplastic appearance.

 

Option D. Adenocarcinoma: Adenocarcinoma is a malignant tumor arising from glandular tissue. It would typically show dysplastic or malignant cells with invasion into surrounding tissues, which are not mentioned in this biopsy report. Given the patient's young age and the benign features described, adenocarcinoma is an unlikely diagnosis.

 

Educational Objective:

questions.stemHtml: Match the following tumors with features correctly:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 1-c, 2-a, 3-d, 4-b

 

  1. Ewing sarcoma → Small round cells with Homer Wright rosettes (c)
    Ewing sarcoma is a highly aggressive bone tumor that typically occurs in children and young adults. It is characterized by small round cells that can form Homer Wright rosettes (a pattern of cells surrounding a central area of neuropil), a key diagnostic feature of this tumor.
  2. Osteoclastoma (Giant cell tumor) → Oval or mononuclear tumor cells with abundant giant cells (a)
    Osteoclastoma, also known as Giant cell tumor of bone, is characterized by oval or mononuclear tumor cells interspersed with abundant giant cells that resemble osteoclasts.
  3. Osteosarcoma → Malignant cells producing osteoid (d)
    Osteosarcoma is a primary bone tumor that produces osteoid (bone matrix). This feature is diagnostic, as the tumor cells are malignant and form bone-like material.
  4. Fibrosarcoma → Spindled cells with herringbone pattern (b)
    Fibrosarcoma is a malignant tumor of fibroblasts. Histologically, it is characterized by spindled cells arranged in a herringbone pattern, a key feature for its diagnosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Ewing sarcoma shows small round cells with Homer Wright rosettes.

 

  • Osteoclastoma (Giant cell tumor) has abundant giant cells.
  • Osteosarcoma is characterized by malignant cells producing osteoid.
  • Fibrosarcoma exhibits spindled cells with a herringbone pattern.

questions.stem: Why do neoplastic cells utilize Warburg metabolism?

options.label: A
options.text: It decreases glucose utilization by neoplastic cells

options.label: B
options.text: It forms metabolic intermediates which are needed for cell growth and multiplication

options.label: C
options.text: It provides more energy in the form of increased ATP production

options.label: D
options.text: It prevents apoptosis and makes the cancer cells immortal

questions.answerText: It forms metabolic intermediates which are needed for cell growth and multiplication
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) It forms metabolic intermediates which are needed for cell growth and multiplication

 

Warburg metabolism, also known as the Warburg effect, describes a metabolic shift in cancer cells where they preferentially use aerobic glycolysis instead of oxidative phosphorylation, even in the presence of oxygen. 

 

Forming metabolic intermediates for cell growth: The Warburg effect allows neoplastic cells to generate metabolic intermediates (such as nucleotides, amino acids, and lipids) that are crucial for the biosynthesis of macromolecules required for rapid cell growth and division. This is the primary reason cancer cells rely on this altered metabolism. Glycolytic intermediates serve as building blocks for anabolic processes, supporting the increased demand for cell components during uncontrolled growth.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It decreases glucose utilization by neoplastic cells: This is incorrect. The Warburg effect actually increases glucose uptake by cancer cells. Neoplastic cells consume large amounts of glucose, which is processed through glycolysis to produce intermediates for cell proliferation.

 

Option C. It provides more energy in the form of increased ATP production: This is incorrect. Glycolysis produces significantly less ATP compared to oxidative phosphorylation. The Warburg effect prioritizes the generation of intermediates for biosynthesis over efficient ATP production.

 

Option D. It prevents apoptosis and makes cancer cells immortal: While the altered metabolism in cancer cells might contribute to their survival and proliferation, the Warburg effect itself is primarily about providing the necessary building blocks for growth, not directly preventing apoptosis or making cells immortal.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Neoplastic cells utilize Warburg metabolism to generate metabolic intermediates that are crucial for the synthesis of macromolecules needed for cell growth and multiplication, rather than maximizing ATP production.

questions.stem: A baby is diagnosed with B cell leukemia. All of the following are good prognostic factors except? HyperdiploidyAge < 1 yeart(9;22)t(4;11)
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) B, C, D

 

In B cell leukemia (especially acute lymphoblastic leukemia, or ALL), there are several prognostic factors that influence outcomes. Some factors are associated with better outcomes, while others indicate a poor prognosis. 

 

B. Age < 1 year: Age less than 1 year is a poor prognostic factor. Infants tend to have more aggressive forms of ALL, often associated with specific genetic abnormalities like MLL rearrangements, which carry a poor prognosis.

 

C. t(9;22): The t(9;22) translocation, also known as the Philadelphia chromosome, is associated with a poor prognosis. This translocation results in the BCR-ABL fusion gene, leading to aggressive disease in both ALL and chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).

 

D. t(4;11): The t(4;11) translocation involves the MLL gene and is also associated with a poor prognosis, particularly in infants. It is linked to aggressive leukemia with a higher likelihood of relapse.

 

Other Options:

 

A. Hyperdiploidy: Hyperdiploidy (having more than the normal 46 chromosomes) is associated with a good prognosis in pediatric ALL. It reflects a more favorable biology of the disease.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The poor prognostic factors in B cell leukemia include age < 1 year, t(9;22) (Philadelphia chromosome), and t(4;11) (MLL rearrangement), while hyperdiploidy is associated with a good prognosis.

questions.stem: A female patient presented with fatigue. Routine complete blood count analysis showed hemoglobin of 9 g/dL, MCV 60 fL, and RBC count of 5.2 million. A peripheral smear showed microcytic hypochromic anemia. Which of the following is the next best investigation for this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) HbA2 levels

 

The patient presents with microcytic hypochromic anemia, which is characterized by a low mean corpuscular volume (MCV) of 60 fL (indicating small red blood cells). Additionally, the RBC count of 5.2 million suggests an elevated or normal RBC count, which can be a clue towards thalassemia rather than iron deficiency anemia.

 

Given this, the most appropriate next step in the diagnostic workup would be to check the HbA2 levels to evaluate for beta-thalassemia trait. An elevated HbA2 level (>3.5%) is indicative of beta-thalassemia trait, a common cause of microcytic anemia with normal or elevated RBC counts.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Serum ferritin levels: Serum ferritin levels would be useful in the diagnosis of iron deficiency anemia (IDA), which also causes microcytic hypochromic anemia. However, the high RBC count makes thalassemia a more likely diagnosis in this case, as iron deficiency typically presents with a low RBC count.

 

Option C. Serum folate levels: Folate deficiency leads to macrocytic anemia (increased MCV), not microcytic anemia. Therefore, measuring serum folate levels would not be appropriate in this case.

 

Option D. Serum homocysteine levels: Elevated homocysteine levels can indicate folate or vitamin B12 deficiency, which also causes macrocytic anemia. Since the patient has microcytic anemia, this test would not be relevant in this context.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In a patient with microcytic hypochromic anemia and an elevated RBC count, the next best investigation is to measure HbA2 levels to evaluate for beta-thalassemia trait, a common cause of microcytic anemia with normal or elevated RBC counts.

questions.stemHtml: A 15-year-old girl presents with a midline neck swelling that moves on deglutition. USG revealed a 2 cm x 2 cm nodule on the left lobe of the thyroid, extending into the strap muscles. The histopathology image is given below. What of the following is not correct about this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased risk with RET/PTC rearrangements and BRAF mutations

options.label: B
options.text: History of childhood radiation exposure with palpable lymph nodes as presentation

options.label: C
options.text: Presence of sheets of polygonal cells which stain positively with Congo red

options.label: D
options.text: Tumor cells have dispersed nuclear chromatin imparting it ground glass or optically clear appearance

questions.answerText: Presence of sheets of polygonal cells which stain positively with Congo red
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Presence of sheets of polygonal cells which stain positively with Congo red

 

The clinical presentation and histopathology are suggestive of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), which is the most common thyroid malignancy in children and young adults. 

 

Presence of sheets of polygonal cells which stain positively with Congo red: False: This description is characteristic of medullary thyroid carcinoma, not papillary thyroid carcinoma. Medullary thyroid carcinoma is associated with Congo red-positive staining due to the presence of amyloid, which is derived from calcitonin secreted by C-cells. PTC does not exhibit these histological features.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Increased risk with RET/PTC rearrangements and BRAF mutations: True: Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is often associated with RET/PTC rearrangements and BRAF mutations, which are common molecular alterations in this type of thyroid cancer. These mutations are important in the pathogenesis of the disease.

 

Option B. History of childhood radiation exposure with palpable lymph nodes as presentation: True: Radiation exposure, especially during childhood, is a significant risk factor for developing PTC. Additionally, palpable lymph nodes are often seen in these patients, as PTC frequently spreads to regional lymph nodes.

 

Option D. Tumor cells have dispersed nuclear chromatin imparting it ground glass or optically clear appearance: True: One of the hallmark features of PTC is the presence of nuclei with ground glass or optically clear chromatin. These nuclei are also described as having Orphan Annie-eye appearance, a characteristic finding in PTC.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Papillary thyroid carcinoma is associated with RET/PTC rearrangements, BRAF mutations, and a history of childhood radiation exposure. It presents with characteristic nuclear features, including ground glass nuclei. The presence of Congo red-positive polygonal cells is more consistent with medullary thyroid carcinoma, not papillary thyroid carcinoma.

questions.stemHtml: An elderly patient presents with anemia and hemoglobinuria. Investigations reveal increased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). The peripheral smear image is given below. Which of the following physical examination findings can support the likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Mechanical second heart sound

 

The peripheral blood smear shows fragmented red blood cells (schistocytes), which are characteristic of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA). Schistocytes form when red blood cells are mechanically fragmented as they pass through small blood vessels with abnormalities, such as in conditions involving prosthetic heart valves or aortic stenosis.

 

Increased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and hemoglobinuria are consistent with intravascular hemolysis, where red blood cells are destroyed within the bloodstream, releasing their contents into the plasma.

 

Mechanical second heart sound suggests the presence of a mechanical heart valve, which is commonly associated with mechanical hemolysis due to the valve causing shear stress on red blood cells, leading to their fragmentation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Splenomegaly: Splenomegaly is often seen in conditions like hereditary spherocytosis or immune hemolytic anemia, where red blood cells are destroyed in the spleen (extravascular hemolysis). However, the presence of schistocytes suggests intravascular hemolysis, which is more consistent with mechanical destruction in the bloodstream rather than splenic involvement.

 

Option B. Frontal bossing: Frontal bossing is commonly seen in thalassemia or other chronic anemias with marrow hyperplasia, leading to skeletal deformities. This finding is not associated with mechanical hemolysis.

 

Option D. Goitre: A goitre is associated with thyroid disorders and has no direct connection to hemolysis or schistocytes. It would not explain the findings in this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In a patient presenting with anemia, hemoglobinuria, and a peripheral smear showing schistocytes, the presence of a mechanical second heart sound suggests that mechanical hemolysis, possibly due to a mechanical heart valve, is the likely diagnosis.

questions.stemHtml: Match the following cell types and the malignancy they are associated with:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c

 

Let's review each of the cell types and the corresponding malignancies:

 

  1. Popcorn cell:
    • Correct match: b (Lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma)
    • The popcorn cell (also called LP cell) is a variant of Reed-Sternberg cells and is seen in lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin’s lymphoma (nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma).
       
  2. Faggot cell:
    • Correct match: a (Acute promyelocytic leukemia)
    • Faggot cells are characteristic of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). These are blast cells filled with bundles of Auer rods.
       
  3. Cerebriform nuclei:
    • Correct match: d (Sezary syndrome)
    • Cerebriform nuclei are seen in Sezary syndrome, which is a leukemic phase of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides). The characteristic appearance of the nucleus resembles the folds of the brain.
       
  4. Starry sky:
    • Correct match: c (Burkitt lymphoma)
    • The starry sky pattern is a classic histological finding in Burkitt lymphoma, characterized by macrophages phagocytizing apoptotic cells, creating a starry appearance amidst the lymphocyte proliferation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Popcorn cells are seen in lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma.
  • Faggot cells are associated with acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL).
  • Cerebriform nuclei are characteristic of Sezary syndrome.
  • Starry sky pattern is a hallmark of Burkitt lymphoma.

 

Thus, the correct answer is A. 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c.

questions.stem: A girl presents with short stature, webbed neck, thick calves, shield-shaped chest, swelling of the ankle, and increased carrying angle. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Turner syndrome

 

The clinical features described in the question align with Turner syndrome, a genetic disorder that affects females and is characterized by the complete or partial absence of one of the X chromosomes (45, X karyotype).

 

  • Short stature is one of the hallmark features of Turner syndrome.
  • Webbed neck is caused by a skin fold that runs along the sides of the neck down to the shoulders, which is a classic feature of Turner syndrome.
  • Shield-shaped chest with widely spaced nipples is another typical characteristic.
  • Swelling of the ankle (lymphedema) is often present at birth or develops in early childhood.
  • Increased carrying angle (cubitus valgus) refers to the outward deviation of the forearm relative to the upper arm, commonly seen in Turner syndrome.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Down syndrome: This genetic disorder is characterized by trisomy 21 and is associated with intellectual disability, hypotonia, and distinctive facial features such as epicanthal folds and a flat nasal bridge. It is not associated with webbed neck, shield chest, or ankle swelling.

 

Option C. Patau syndrome: This is trisomy 13, characterized by severe intellectual disability, cleft lip and palate, microcephaly, and polydactyly, but not by the features described in the question.

 

Option D. Edward syndrome: This is trisomy 18, which presents with severe developmental delay, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, and rocker-bottom feet, but does not match the features listed here.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Turner syndrome is characterized by features such as short stature, webbed neck, shield-shaped chest, and lymphedema, making it the most likely diagnosis in this case.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding clear cell carcinoma of the kidney? It is the most common sporadic renal tumorAssociated with loss of long arm of chromosome 3Arises from distal convoluted tubuleCells show intracellular accumulation of glycogen and fat
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 1, 4

 

Clear cell carcinoma of the kidney, also called clear cell renal cell carcinoma (RCC), is the most common type of renal cancer. 

 

1. It is the most common sporadic renal tumor: This is true. Clear cell carcinoma is the most frequent histologic subtype of renal cell carcinoma, representing 70-80% of all renal tumors, particularly in sporadic cases.

 

4. Cells show intracellular accumulation of glycogen and fat: This is true. The name "clear cell carcinoma" comes from the characteristic appearance of the tumor cells, which contain abundant glycogen and lipids. These substances are dissolved during tissue processing, leaving the cells with a clear appearance under the microscope.

 

Other Options:

 

2. Associated with loss of long arm of chromosome 3: This statement is true, but it's not part of the correct answer combination (D). Clear cell RCC is strongly associated with loss of the short arm of chromosome 3p (not the long arm), involving the VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) gene. This genetic mutation plays a major role in the development of the tumor, but the key fact here is its involvement in the short arm of chromosome 3.

 

3. Arises from distal convoluted tubule: This is false. Clear cell RCC originates from the proximal convoluted tubule, not the distal convoluted tubule.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Clear cell carcinoma is the most common type of sporadic renal tumor.
  • The tumor cells show intracellular accumulation of glycogen and fat, giving them a characteristic clear appearance under the microscope.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a poor prognostic marker of multiple myeloma?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) β-2 microglobulin

 

Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell malignancy, and several markers are used to assess prognosis in patients. Among these, β-2 microglobulin is considered one of the most important poor prognostic markers.

 

β-2 microglobulin: β-2 microglobulin is a protein found on the surface of most nucleated cells and is released into the blood when cells, particularly cancerous plasma cells, are destroyed. High levels of β-2 microglobulin in the blood are associated with advanced disease and poor prognosis in multiple myeloma. It reflects both tumor burden and kidney function (as it is cleared by the kidneys). It is part of the International Staging System (ISS) for multiple myeloma prognosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Calcium levels: Hypercalcemia is a feature of advanced multiple myeloma due to bone resorption from osteolytic lesions, but while high calcium levels indicate disease activity, they are not specifically used as a primary prognostic marker.

 

Option C. Serum creatinine: Elevated creatinine indicates kidney dysfunction, which can occur in multiple myeloma due to the effects of light chains on the kidneys (cast nephropathy). While renal failure worsens the clinical course, serum β-2 microglobulin is more directly associated with prognosis.

 

Option D. Protein levels: Elevated levels of monoclonal proteins (M-protein) in the blood or urine indicate disease activity in multiple myeloma, but total protein levels are not as closely linked to prognosis as β-2 microglobulin.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In multiple myeloma, elevated β-2 microglobulin is a significant poor prognostic marker, as it reflects both tumor burden and renal function. Other factors like calcium and creatinine levels are important in disease management but are not as strong predictors of prognosis.

questions.stem: Donor blood should be screened for the following infections except?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Dengue virus


Blood is not routinely screened for dengue virus. While dengue can be transmitted via blood in rare cases, its screening is not typically included in standard blood donation protocols due to its transient viremia and the lower risk of transmission compared to viruses like HIV, HBV, and HCV.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hepatitis C virus: Screening for Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is mandatory because this virus can be transmitted through blood transfusions, and chronic HCV infection can lead to severe liver diseases such as cirrhosis and liver cancer.

 

Option C. Human immunodeficiency virus: Screening for HIV is also required to prevent transmission of the virus, which can lead to AIDS in recipients. HIV screening is an essential part of blood safety protocols worldwide.

 

Option D. Hepatitis B virus: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) screening is critical because HBV is easily transmitted through blood and can cause both acute and chronic liver disease.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Donor blood is routinely screened for HIV, Hepatitis B, and Hepatitis C. However, Dengue virus is not part of standard screening protocols for blood donations.

questions.stem: A child is presenting with palpable blanching purpura, abdominal pain, and pain in the knee joint resulting from arthritis. Urine examination showed hematuria and proteinuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Henoch-Schonlein purpura

 

Henoch-Schonlein Purpura (HSP), also known as IgA vasculitis, is the most common form of systemic vasculitis in children. It is characterized by IgA immune complex deposition in small blood vessels, leading to a range of symptoms, which include:

 

  1. Palpable purpura (typically on the lower extremities and buttocks): The purpura in HSP is non-thrombocytopenic, meaning that platelet counts are usually normal, unlike in other purpuric conditions such as immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).
  2. Abdominal pain: Due to vasculitis affecting the gastrointestinal tract, patients may experience abdominal pain, which is often crampy and can be associated with gastrointestinal bleeding.
  3. Arthritis/Arthralgia: Pain in the joints, especially the knees and ankles, is common in HSP.
  4. Hematuria and proteinuria: Kidney involvement occurs due to IgA nephropathy, leading to blood (hematuria) and protein (proteinuria) in the urine.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP): ITP presents with purpura due to a low platelet count, but it does not typically involve abdominal pain, arthritis, or kidney issues (hematuria/proteinuria). ITP usually results in isolated thrombocytopenia without systemic symptoms.

 

Option B. Dengue: Dengue fever can present with a rash, joint pain (arthralgia), and low platelets (thrombocytopenia), but abdominal pain and kidney involvement (hematuria/proteinuria) are not characteristic of typical dengue presentations.

 

Option C. Churg-Strauss syndrome: Churg-Strauss syndrome (also known as eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis) involves eosinophilia, asthma, and allergic rhinitis. It can cause vasculitis but usually presents in adults rather than children, and its features do not closely align with those of HSP.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Henoch-Schonlein Purpura (HSP) is characterized by palpable purpura, abdominal pain, joint pain, and kidney involvement (hematuria and proteinuria). It is the most common cause of vasculitis in children and involves IgA deposition in small blood vessels.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old female patient is diagnosed with pure red cell aplasia and a mediastinal mass. Which of the following can be the likely cause?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Thymoma

 

Pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) is a rare disorder characterized by a selective reduction in red blood cell precursors in the bone marrow, leading to anemia with normal white blood cell and platelet counts. It can be associated with various conditions, but a strong connection exists between PRCA and thymoma.


Thymoma, a tumor of the thymus gland, located in the mediastinum, is often associated with autoimmune conditions, including pure red cell aplasia and myasthenia gravis. The thymus plays an important role in immune regulation, and thymomas can lead to aberrant immune responses, including the production of antibodies that attack erythroid precursors in the bone marrow, causing PRCA. The presence of a mediastinal mass makes thymoma the most likely diagnosis in this case.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma can present as a mediastinal mass, especially in cases like primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma. However, it is typically associated with lymphadenopathy, fever, weight loss, and other systemic symptoms. It is not strongly associated with pure red cell aplasia (PRCA), which makes this less likely in this case.

 

Option C. Bronchogenic carcinoma: Bronchogenic carcinoma refers to lung cancer, which can present with a mediastinal mass if the tumor spreads or invades nearby tissues. However, bronchogenic carcinoma is not commonly linked to pure red cell aplasia. Lung cancers are more frequently associated with paraneoplastic syndromes like hypercalcemia or SIADH, but PRCA is unusual.

 

Option D. Germ cell tumor: Germ cell tumors, particularly mediastinal germ cell tumors, are more commonly seen in young males and can present with a mediastinal mass. These tumors, however, are not typically associated with pure red cell aplasia. While germ cell tumors can cause mass effects or secrete markers like alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) or beta-hCG, they are less likely to be associated with hematologic abnormalities like PRCA.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Among the given options, thymoma is the most likely cause of pure red cell aplasia in a patient with a mediastinal mass, as thymomas are strongly associated with autoimmune diseases like PRCA. Other conditions such as Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, bronchogenic carcinoma, and germ cell tumors are less likely to be linked to this specific hematologic presentation.

Match the following microscopic finding with the type of tumor:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b

 

  1. Schiller-Duval bodies (Yolk sac tumor) – Schiller-Duval bodies are a histological feature specific to yolk sac tumors (also called endodermal sinus tumors). These structures resemble glomeruli and are a hallmark of this tumor.
  2. Presence of teeth, hair, cartilage (Teratoma) – The presence of mature tissues like teeth, hair, and cartilage is characteristic of teratomas, which are germ cell tumors that contain elements from multiple germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm).
  3. Signet ring cells (Kruckenberg tumor) – Signet ring cells are commonly seen in Kruckenberg tumors, which are metastatic tumors in the ovary, often originating from the stomach.
  4. Call-Exner bodies (Granulosa cell tumor) – Call-Exner bodies are seen in granulosa cell tumors of the ovary. These are small, eosinophilic, follicle-like structures.
