questions.stem: Which of the following statements is false regarding neutrophil extracellular trapping (NET)?

options.label: A
options.text: It is detected in blood during sepsis

options.label: C
options.text: It is associated with inactivation of arginine deiminase

options.label: D
options.text: It is chromatin with antibacterial enzymes

questions.answerText: It is associated with inactivation of arginine deiminase
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) It is associated with inactivation of arginine deiminase

 

Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are formed when neutrophils release their chromatin material along with antimicrobial proteins to trap and kill pathogens. The enzyme peptidylarginine deiminase 4 (PAD4) plays a critical role in NET formation by citrullinating histones, which leads to chromatin decondensation. Arginine deiminase, or PAD4, is activated in NET formation, not inactivated, making option C false.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It is detected in blood during sepsis: This is true. NETs are often detected in the blood during sepsis. In sepsis, the formation of NETs is a mechanism by which the body attempts to trap and kill pathogens. However, excessive NET formation can contribute to complications like thrombosis and organ damage.

 

Option B. Mitochondrial DNA is not involved: This statement is false, making it another good candidate if mitochondrial DNA were to be included in NET formation. However, mitochondrial DNA is involved in certain types of NET formation under non-lytic conditions, where the neutrophils release mitochondrial DNA instead of nuclear DNA.

 

Option D. It is chromatin with antibacterial enzymes: This is true. NETs consist of decondensed chromatin (primarily nuclear DNA) that is coated with antibacterial proteins like elastase, myeloperoxidase, and cathepsin G. These enzymes help to neutralize and kill pathogens trapped within the NET structure.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), the enzyme PAD4 is activated, not inactivated, which is necessary for chromatin decondensation and NET formation. NETs are also found in sepsis, can involve mitochondrial DNA, and consist of chromatin with antibacterial enzymes to fight pathogens.

questions.stem: What can be the mechanism by which the phagolysosome causes cell death in autophagy?

options.label: A
options.text: Is both intra and extra cellular

options.label: B
options.text: Can fuse with other organelles directly

options.label: C
options.text: Fuses with lysosome to form autophagolysosome

options.label: D
options.text: It is a single membrane structure

questions.answerText: Fuses with lysosome to form autophagolysosome
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Fuses with lysosome to form autophagolysosome

 

In the process of autophagy, a phagosome (or autophagosome) forms and engulfs damaged organelles or cellular components. This autophagosome then fuses with a lysosome to form an autophagolysosome, where the contents are degraded by lysosomal enzymes. This is a critical step in the degradation and recycling of cellular materials, and in cases of excessive autophagy, it can lead to cell death by overwhelming the cell’s ability to maintain homeostasis.

 

  • Phagolysosome formation involves the fusion of the autophagosome with the lysosome, which is key to the degradation process.

 

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Is both intra and extracellular: Autophagy is an intracellular process that occurs within the cell. It does not involve extracellular mechanisms.

 

Option B. Can fuse with other organelles directly: While autophagosomes may engulf damaged organelles, they do not fuse with organelles directly. Instead, they fuse with lysosomes to form autophagolysosomes for degradation.

 

Option D. It is a single membrane structure: The autophagosome is a double-membrane structure, not single membrane. The double membrane is one of the distinguishing features of autophagosomes in the autophagic process.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In autophagy, the autophagosome fuses with a lysosome to form an autophagolysosome, where cellular materials are degraded. This process is essential for the breakdown and recycling of damaged organelles and can lead to cell death if autophagy is excessive.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old patient presented to the clinic with a history of malabsorption, diarrhea, and poor appetite. He has been diagnosed with celiac sprue after thorough workup. Which of the following statements is incorrect about this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Crypt hyperplasia, villi atrophy and CD8+ cells in lamina propria are classical findings

options.label: B
options.text: Duodenal biopsy of the patient shows normal mucosal thickness

options.label: C
options.text: Dietary substitution can improve the condition of the patient

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Protective for GI lymphoma

 

Celiac disease (also known as celiac sprue) is an autoimmune disorder triggered by the ingestion of gluten in genetically predisposed individuals. It primarily affects the small intestine, leading to malabsorption, diarrhea, and nutritional deficiencies. Here's why option D is incorrect:

 

Protective for GI lymphoma: This is false. In fact, celiac disease is associated with an increased risk of gastrointestinal (GI) lymphoma, specifically enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL). Long-standing or untreated celiac disease is linked to a higher risk of lymphoma, making this option incorrect.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Crypt hyperplasia, villi atrophy, and CD8+ cells in lamina propria are classical findings: This is true. The classic histological features of celiac disease include villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and an infiltration of CD8+ T cells in the lamina propria. These findings are usually seen on duodenal biopsy and are critical for diagnosing celiac disease.

 

Option B. Duodenal biopsy of the patient shows normal mucosal thickness: This is true. While celiac disease causes villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia, the overall mucosal thickness typically remains normal. The mucosal structure is altered due to damage but not necessarily thinned overall.

 

Option C. Dietary substitution can improve the condition of the patient: This is true. The primary treatment for celiac disease is a gluten-free diet, which leads to significant improvement in symptoms and mucosal healing. Strict adherence to a gluten-free diet can reverse the intestinal damage and improve nutritional deficiencies.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Celiac disease is associated with an increased risk of gastrointestinal lymphoma (especially enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma), and a gluten-free diet can significantly improve the condition. Classical biopsy findings include villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and infiltration of CD8+ T cells.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct logical sequence?

options.label: A
options.text: Bedside blood collection, label the samples, fill the laboratory requisition forms, Identify the patient

options.label: B
options.text: Fill the laboratory requisition forms, Identify the Patient, Bedside blood collection, label the samples

options.label: C
options.text: Label the sample tubes, Bedside blood collection, fill the laboratory requisition forms, Identify the patient

options.label: D
options.text: Identify the Patient, Fill the laboratory requisition forms, Bedside blood collection, label the samples

questions.answerText: Fill the laboratory requisition forms, Identify the Patient, Bedside blood collection, label the samples
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Fill the laboratory requisition forms, Identify the Patient, Bedside blood collection, label the samples

 

The correct logical sequence for blood sample collection in a medical setting follows specific steps to ensure safety, accuracy, and compliance with laboratory protocols:

 

  1. Fill the laboratory requisition forms: The first step is to fill out the laboratory requisition form. This document lists the tests to be performed, provides patient information, and ensures that the lab is aware of what needs to be done with the sample. This form must be completed before proceeding with the collection to avoid confusion or omissions.
  2. Identify the Patient: Patient identification is critical and must occur before any procedure is done. Correctly identifying the patient ensures that the right person is being tested and prevents serious errors. The requisition form should match the patient’s information.
  3. Bedside blood collection: Once the patient is correctly identified, the blood sample can be collected at the bedside using appropriate sterile techniques.
  4. Label the samples: After collecting the sample, it is important to immediately label the tubes with the patient’s information, including name, date of birth, and the date and time of collection. Proper labeling ensures that the sample is accurately traced back to the patient.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The correct sequence for safe and effective blood collection starts with filling out the laboratory requisition form, followed by identifying the patient, collecting the blood sample, and finally labeling the sample properly. This ensures all necessary steps are followed for accuracy in diagnostics.

questions.stem: L & H type Reed-Sternberg (RS) cells are seen with:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Lymphocyte predominant

 

L & H type Reed-Sternberg (RS) cells, also known as "popcorn cells," are characteristic of Nodular Lymphocyte-Predominant Hodgkin Lymphoma (NLPHL), a subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma. These cells have a lobulated nucleus resembling popcorn and are a hallmark feature that helps distinguish this subtype from Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma (CHL), which has the more typical classical Reed-Sternberg cells.

 

Lymphocyte predominant: Nodular Lymphocyte-Predominant Hodgkin Lymphoma (NLPHL) is characterized by L & H cells (popcorn cells). This subtype has a relatively good prognosis and is distinct from classical Hodgkin lymphoma due to its unique cell morphology and clinical presentation. These cells express CD20, a B-cell marker, unlike the Reed-Sternberg cells in classical Hodgkin lymphoma.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Mixed cellular type: This is a subtype of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma and typically contains classical Reed-Sternberg cells, not the L & H type. The mixed cellular type is associated with a mixture of inflammatory cells and RS cells.

 

Option B. Nodular sclerosis: Nodular sclerosis is the most common subtype of Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma and features lacunar Reed-Sternberg cells, not the L & H type. This subtype presents with bands of fibrosis and is common in young adults.

 

Option D. Classical Hodgkin lymphoma: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, including the mixed cellular type and nodular sclerosis, is characterized by classical Reed-Sternberg cells rather than the L & H type seen in Nodular Lymphocyte-Predominant Hodgkin Lymphoma.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The L & H type Reed-Sternberg cells (popcorn cells) are a defining feature of Nodular Lymphocyte-Predominant Hodgkin Lymphoma (NLPHL), distinguishing it from Classical Hodgkin Lymphoma subtypes, which contain the more typical classical Reed-Sternberg cells.

questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old male patient is brought to the OPD with severe breathlessness. On echocardiography, mitral stenosis with left atrial hypertrophy is seen. Vegetations present on the mitral valve were excised. What could be the most likely diagnosis based on the given histopathological examination finding?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Rheumatic valvular disease

 

The image provided shows Aschoff bodies, which are pathognomonic for rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease (RHD). This histopathological finding features collections of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by lymphocytes, macrophages, and Anitschkow cells (activated macrophages with a wavy, caterpillar-like nucleus).

 

The clinical scenario of mitral stenosis with left atrial hypertrophy and vegetations is also characteristic of rheumatic heart disease, which results from recurrent episodes of acute rheumatic fever, often following a streptococcal infection (e.g., group A streptococcus).

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Infective endocarditis: Infective endocarditis usually presents with larger, more destructive vegetations, which consist of fibrin, bacteria, and inflammatory cells. The histopathological features of infective endocarditis are not seen in the provided image.

 

Option C. Myxoma: Cardiac myxomas are benign tumors typically found in the left atrium. They are composed of myxoid stroma and stellate cells but would not show the features seen in the histological image.

 

Option D. Sarcoidosis: Sarcoidosis is characterized by non-caseating granulomas, which are not visible in this histopathological sample. It primarily affects the lungs but can involve the heart, usually leading to arrhythmias rather than valvular disease.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The combination of mitral stenosis, left atrial hypertrophy, and the histopathological finding of Aschoff bodies strongly suggests rheumatic valvular disease, a sequela of rheumatic fever.

questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old man suffering from persistent fatigue and lymph node enlargement visits the outpatient department. Examination of his peripheral smear reveals the image as shown. Which of the following is not true about his condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Originates from a naïve B cell

options.label: B
options.text: Monoclonal lymphocytosis of uncertain significance is considered to be a precursor lesion

options.label: C
options.text: Hypergammaglobulinemia is common due to neoplastic B cell proliferation

options.label: D
options.text: Flow cytometry should be done for confirmation of diagnosis

questions.answerText: Hypergammaglobulinemia is common due to neoplastic B cell proliferation
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Hypergammaglobulinemia is common due to neoplastic B cell proliferation

 

The image provided and the clinical presentation of an elderly patient with persistent fatigue, lymphadenopathy, and a peripheral smear showing smudge cells are highly suggestive of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). 

 

Hypergammaglobulinemia is common due to neoplastic B cell proliferation (False): This statement is incorrect. In CLL, neoplastic B cells do not function properly. Instead of hypergammaglobulinemia (excessive production of antibodies), patients with CLL often develop hypogammaglobulinemia (low levels of immunoglobulins), leading to increased susceptibility to infections. The dysfunctional B cells fail to produce adequate amounts of immunoglobulins.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Originates from a naïve B cell (True): CLL is a B-cell neoplasm that typically arises from a naïve B cell or sometimes a memory B cell. These cells accumulate in the blood, bone marrow, and lymphoid tissues.

 

Option B. Monoclonal lymphocytosis of uncertain significance is considered to be a precursor lesion (True): Monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (MBL) is considered a precursor condition to CLL. Patients with MBL have an elevated number of monoclonal B cells but without the full-blown clinical features of CLL. Many cases of MBL may progress to CLL over time.

 

Option D. Flow cytometry should be done for confirmation of diagnosis (True): Flow cytometry is a critical diagnostic tool for CLL. It helps confirm the diagnosis by identifying the characteristic immunophenotype of CLL cells, which typically express markers like CD5, CD19, CD20, and CD23.

 

Educational Objective:

 

While hypogammaglobulinemia is common in CLL due to the dysfunctional nature of the neoplastic B cells, hypergammaglobulinemia is not a feature of CLL.

questions.stem: The clotting factors present in high concentration in cryoprecipitate are: Von Willebrand factorFactor XIIIFibrinogenThrombin
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 1, 2 and 3

 

Cryoprecipitate is a blood product derived from fresh frozen plasma (FFP) by thawing at 1-6 °C and contains a concentrated portion of several key clotting factors. It is used in the treatment of bleeding disorders, especially those involving deficiencies in specific clotting proteins. 

 

Clotting Factors Present in High Concentration in Cryoprecipitate:

 

  1. Von Willebrand Factor (vWF)
  2. Factor VIII (especially vWF-bound form)
  3. Fibrinogen (Factor I)
  4. Factor XIII

 

The main components of cryoprecipitate include:

 

1. Von Willebrand factor (vWF): This is present in high concentrations in cryoprecipitate and is essential for platelet adhesion and aggregation, playing a crucial role in primary hemostasis.

 

2. Factor XIII: Cryoprecipitate contains factor XIII, which is important for stabilizing the fibrin clot by cross-linking fibrin fibers, enhancing clot strength.

 

3. Fibrinogen: This is another important component of cryoprecipitate. Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin during the coagulation process, and its administration helps in situations like hypofibrinogenemia or massive bleeding.

 

Other Options:

 

4. Thrombin: Thrombin is not present in high concentrations in cryoprecipitate. Thrombin is a separate enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin but is not concentrated in cryoprecipitate. It is produced in the final steps of the coagulation cascade.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cryoprecipitate contains high concentrations of von Willebrand factor, factor XIII, and fibrinogen, but thrombin is not significantly present. Therefore, the correct answer is C. 1, 2 and 3.



ore, the correct answer is C. 1, 2 and 3.

questions.stem: In a known case of breast cancer, Fluorescent In-Situ Hybridization (FISH) for gene amplification will be done based on which of the following immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining for HER2/Neu?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 2

 

HER2/Neu (human epidermal growth factor receptor 2) is a protein that, when overexpressed or amplified, is associated with certain aggressive forms of breast cancer. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) is typically the first step in testing for HER2 status.

 

The IHC scoring system for HER2 is as follows:

 

  • 0 or 1+: Negative for HER2 overexpression.
  • 2+: Equivocal. This result is indeterminate and requires further testing (usually FISH) to determine if HER2 gene amplification is present.
  • 3+: Positive for HER2 overexpression. No further testing (such as FISH) is typically required because this score indicates HER2 positivity.

 

In cases where the IHC score is 2+, FISH (Fluorescent In-Situ Hybridization) is recommended to assess HER2 gene amplification and confirm whether HER2-targeted therapy (such as trastuzumab) would be effective.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. 1: This score indicates a negative result for HER2 overexpression, and further testing (like FISH) is usually not required.

 

Option C. 3: This score is positive for HER2 overexpression, so FISH is not needed as the result already indicates HER2 positivity.

 

Option D. Any of the above: Incorrect, as only an IHC score of 2+ (equivocal) necessitates further testing via FISH.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In breast cancer, FISH testing for HER2 gene amplification is typically performed when the IHC score is 2+ (equivocal) to clarify HER2 status and guide treatment decisions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is incorrect about invasive lobular carcinoma of the breast?

options.label: A
options.text: It is presenting as an occult primary

options.label: B
options.text: It is associated with familial gastric cancer

options.label: C
options.text: There is over-activity of CDH1 gene

options.label: D
options.text: It tends to be multifocal and bilateral.

questions.answerText: There is over-activity of CDH1 gene
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) There is over-activity of CDH1 gene

 

Invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC) of the breast is associated with a mutation in the CDH1 gene, which encodes the protein E-cadherin. This mutation leads to a loss of function rather than overactivity. E-cadherin is essential for cell adhesion, and its inactivation promotes the spread of lobular carcinoma cells in a single-file pattern. Therefore, the statement “There is over-activity of CDH1 gene” is incorrect.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It is presenting as an occult primary: ILC can present as an occult primary, meaning it might not form a distinct lump, making it harder to detect on physical exams or imaging.

 

Option B. It is associated with familial gastric cancer: Mutations in the CDH1 gene are linked to an increased risk of both invasive lobular carcinoma of the breast and hereditary diffuse gastric cancer.

 

Option D. It tends to be multifocal and bilateral: ILC has a higher likelihood of being multifocal (occurring in multiple areas within the same breast) and bilateral (affecting both breasts).

 

Educational Objective:

 

Invasive lobular carcinoma is linked to a loss of function mutation in the CDH1 gene, which leads to decreased E-cadherin activity, promoting tumor spread.



ore, the statement “There is over-activity of CDH1 gene” is incorrect. Other Options: Option A. It is presenting as an occult primary: ILC can present as an occult primary, meaning it might not form a distinct lump, making it harder to detect on physical exams or imaging. Option B. It is associated with familial gastric cancer: Mutations in the CDH1 gene are linked to an increased risk of both invasive lobular carcinoma of the breast and hereditary diffuse gastric cancer. Option D. It tends to be multifocal and bilateral: ILC has a higher likelihood of being multifocal (occurring in multiple areas within the same breast) and bilateral (affecting both breasts). Educational Objective: Invasive lobular carcinoma is linked to a loss of function mutation in the CDH1 gene, which leads to decreased E-cadherin activity, promoting tumor spread.

questions.stem: Which one is not helpful in DNA double-strand break repair?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) MSH 2

 

DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are one of the most severe forms of DNA damage and can lead to genomic instability. There are two main pathways to repair these breaks: homologous recombination (HR) and non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). The proteins involved in these pathways are essential for maintaining genomic integrity.

 

MSH2: MSH2 is not involved in double-strand break repair but is crucial for single-strand DNA repair in the mismatch repair pathway.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. ATM (Ataxia Telangiectasia Mutated): ATM is a key regulator of the DNA damage response and is activated by double-strand breaks. It helps initiate repair by phosphorylating several proteins involved in DSB repair, including BRCA1. Thus, ATM plays a critical role in DSB repair.

 

Option B. BRCA1 (Breast Cancer 1): BRCA1 is involved in homologous recombination (HR), a high-fidelity repair mechanism for double-strand breaks. It helps mediate the repair of DSBs by recruiting other proteins to the site of damage, making BRCA1 essential for this process.

 

Option C. Ku 70: Ku 70 is a protein that binds to the broken DNA ends during non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). Together with Ku 80, it forms the Ku complex, which is crucial for the NHEJ pathway, a rapid but error-prone method of DSB repair.

 

Educational Objective:

 

While ATM, BRCA1, and Ku 70 are all involved in DNA double-strand break repair, MSH2 functions primarily in mismatch repair and is not involved in DSB repair.

questions.stem: Which of the following contributes to the pathogenesis of a 47-year-old male with 400 ml urine output in 24 hours and having crescents on histology with pauci-immune glomerulonephritis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) ANCA

 

The patient's presentation with oliguria, crescents on histology, and pauci-immune glomerulonephritis is highly suggestive of ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV), such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) or microscopic polyangiitis (MPA).

 

  • ANCA (Anti-Neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibodies) are responsible for neutrophil activation, leading to inflammation and damage in glomeruli, causing pauci-immune glomerulonephritis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Anti-GBM antibody: Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome) causes linear deposits of IgG on the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), which would show up on immunofluorescence. It is not associated with pauci-immune glomerulonephritis.

 

Option B. Anti-nuclear antibody: Anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) are typically associated with lupus nephritis, which is an immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis, not pauci-immune.

 

Option C. Anti-phospholipase A2 receptor antibody: This antibody is specific for membranous nephropathy, which presents with immune complex deposition in the glomeruli and does not cause crescentic or pauci-immune glomerulonephritis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The pauci-immune nature of the glomerulonephritis and the presence of crescents strongly suggest an ANCA-associated vasculitis as the underlying cause.

questions.stem: A young female of 25-year-old presented with a bleeding disorder. On taking a detailed history, she expressed that her father and sister also have the same bleeding disorders. Which is the most likely disorder in her?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) von Willebrand disease

 

Von Willebrand disease (vWD) is the most likely diagnosis in this case, given the autosomal inheritance pattern and the fact that both males and females in the family are affected. vWD is the most common inherited bleeding disorder and affects both genders equally. It is caused by a deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor (vWF), which plays a critical role in platelet adhesion and stabilization of factor VIII.

 

Key points:

 

  • Both males and females are affected (as seen in the patient’s father and sister).
  • It is the most common bleeding disorder.
  • vWD can present with mucocutaneous bleeding, easy bruising, and prolonged bleeding time.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hemophilia A: Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder, typically affecting males, with females being carriers. Since the patient is female and the disease is present in both her father and sister, Hemophilia A is less likely.

 

Option B. Christmas disease: Also known as Hemophilia B, this is another X-linked recessive disorder affecting mostly males. The inheritance pattern described (both a father and a sister being affected) is inconsistent with an X-linked condition.

 

Option D. Factor XI deficiency: Factor XI deficiency is inherited in either an autosomal dominant or recessive pattern and affects both genders. However, it is much rarer than von Willebrand disease, making it a less likely diagnosis in this scenario.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Von Willebrand disease is the most likely diagnosis in a young female with a bleeding disorder affecting both males and females in the family, following an autosomal inheritance pattern.

questions.stem: Pick the correct statements about hemolytic anemia: Sickle cell anemia has high osmotic fragility and high mechanical fragilityIncreased HbA2 is seen with iron deficiency anemiaMentzer index helps in the differentiation of thalassemia trait from iron deficiency anemiaDonath Landsteiner antibody is seen in cold hemolysin disease
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 3 and 4

 

3. Mentzer index helps in the differentiation of thalassemia trait from iron deficiency anemia:
This is correct. The Mentzer index is calculated as the MCV (mean corpuscular volume) divided by the RBC count. A Mentzer index of <13 suggests thalassemia, while an index of >13 suggests iron deficiency anemia.

 

4. Donath Landsteiner antibody is seen in cold hemolysin disease:
This is correct. The Donath-Landsteiner antibody is a characteristic finding in paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH), which is also known as cold hemolysin disease. It is an autoantibody that binds to RBCs in cold temperatures and causes hemolysis upon rewarming.

 

Other Options:

 

1. Sickle cell anemia has high osmotic fragility and high mechanical fragility: This is incorrect. Sickle cells have high mechanical fragility but low osmotic fragility. They are more prone to mechanical damage as they pass through narrow capillaries, but they are less susceptible to osmotic lysis.

 

2. Increased HbA2 is seen with iron deficiency anemia: This is incorrect. Increased HbA2 is a characteristic of beta-thalassemia trait, not iron deficiency anemia. In iron deficiency anemia, HbA2 levels are usually normal or even decreased.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • The Mentzer index helps differentiate thalassemia trait from iron deficiency anemia.
  • Donath-Landsteiner antibody is a marker for cold hemolysin disease (paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria).

questions.stem: A 60-year-old vegetarian patient presented with weakness and reduced work capacity. He had a hemoglobin of 10g/dl and MCV of 110. He is most likely to have which of the following diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Megaloblastic anemia

 

The patient's hemoglobin of 10 g/dl and MCV of 110 indicate macrocytic anemia (increased mean corpuscular volume). A macrocytic anemia with an elevated MCV (>100) is commonly seen in megaloblastic anemia, which is typically due to a deficiency of vitamin B12 or folate.

 

Key points:

 

  • The patient is vegetarian, and vitamin B12 deficiency is common in vegetarians due to low intake of animal products.
  • Weakness and reduced work capacity are common symptoms of anemia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Iron deficiency anemia: Typically presents with microcytic anemia (low MCV).

 

Option B. Aplastic anemia: A rare condition with pancytopenia (low counts of all blood cells), but not specifically associated with macrocytosis.

 

Option D. Thalassemia: Generally presents with microcytic anemia (low MCV), not macrocytosis.

 

Educational Objectives:

 

The most likely diagnosis is Megaloblastic anemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency, especially considering the patient's vegetarian diet.

questions.stem: A Punjabi patient complains of tiredness and was investigated. He has microcytic hypochromic red cells on peripheral smear. His RDW was increased, and RBC count was low. Which of the following is the further investigation to confirm the diagnosis of this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Serum ferritin studies

 

The combination of microcytic hypochromic red cells, increased red cell distribution width (RDW), and low RBC count raises suspicion for iron deficiency anemia (IDA), which is the most common cause of microcytic anemia, especially in populations where iron deficiency is prevalent.

 

  • Serum ferritin studies: Ferritin is a measure of iron stores in the body. Serum ferritin levels are typically low in iron deficiency anemia, making this test the most appropriate next step to confirm iron deficiency as the cause of this patient's microcytic hypochromic anemia. Ferritin levels would be decreased, supporting a diagnosis of IDA.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Globin gene sequencing: This test is used to diagnose thalassemias and other hemoglobinopathies, which can also present with microcytic anemia. However, based on the patient's increased RDW and low RBC count, iron deficiency anemia is more likely. Thalassemia typically presents with normal or slightly increased RBC count.

 

Option B. HbA2 estimation: This test is used to diagnose beta-thalassemia minor, where HbA2 levels are elevated. While thalassemia is a differential diagnosis for microcytic hypochromic anemia, the low RBC count and increased RDW in this patient are more consistent with iron deficiency anemia rather than thalassemia.

 

Option D. Osmotic fragility: This test is used to diagnose hereditary spherocytosis, which typically presents with normocytic or slightly macrocytic anemia, rather than microcytic hypochromic anemia. It is not the appropriate test for this presentation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

For a patient with microcytic hypochromic anemia, increased RDW, and low RBC count, the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis is serum ferritin studies, which will help determine if iron deficiency anemia is the underlying cause.

The red line in the graph represents an increase in osmotic fragility. This means that the red blood cells (RBCs) in this condition are more prone to lysis when exposed to decreasing concentrations of NaCl (hypotonic solutions).

 

In conditions where the RBCs have altered shapes, such as being more spherical or more fragile, the osmotic fragility increases, causing them to burst at higher concentrations of NaCl compared to normal cells.

 

2. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) can also lead to increased osmotic fragility as the immune-mediated destruction of RBC membranes makes them more fragile.

 

3. Hereditary spherocytosis is characterized by the presence of spherical RBCs due to a defect in the cytoskeletal proteins. These spherical cells are less deformable and more fragile, leading to increased osmotic fragility, which is what the red line represents.

 

Other Options:

 

Option 1. Sickle cell anemia: Sickle cell anemia primarily involves RBCs that become sickle-shaped under low oxygen conditions. However, sickle cells tend to have decreased, not increased, osmotic fragility. Therefore, it does not match the condition represented by the red line.

questions.stem: The phlebotomist needs to collect samples from a patient for various tests. Among the options provided, which sequence of blood collection for testing ensures that the sample remains uncontaminated, considering the additives present in the collection tubes?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Light blue → Red → Lavender → Grey

 

In blood sample collection, it is essential to follow a specific order of draw to prevent cross-contamination between the additives present in different collection tubes. If not followed, the results of the tests could be compromised. The correct order of draw minimizes the risk of additive carryover and ensures sample integrity.

 

The correct sequence based on the additives is as follows:

 

  1. Light blue (Citrate tube): This tube is used for coagulation studies and must be drawn first to avoid contamination by other additives, especially clot activators or EDTA, which could interfere with clotting times.
  2. Red (Serum tube): These tubes are either plain or have clot activators but contain no anticoagulants. Drawing the serum tube after the light blue tube ensures that coagulation tests are unaffected.
  3. Lavender (EDTA tube): EDTA is a potent anticoagulant used for hematology tests (e.g., complete blood count). If drawn earlier, EDTA could interfere with coagulation or serum tests.
  4. Grey (Fluoride/Oxalate tube): This tube contains sodium fluoride, which inhibits glycolysis, and is typically used for glucose testing. It must be drawn last to prevent contamination with anticoagulants that could affect other tests.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The correct sequence of blood sample collection is Light blue → Red → Lavender → Grey, ensuring proper sample integrity and avoiding contamination by additives from different tubes.

Ans. C) 1, 2, 3

 

Amyloidosis is a group of diseases characterized by the deposition of abnormal protein aggregates, known as amyloid, in various tissues and organs. 

 

1. It is an extracellular protein: Amyloid is deposited in the extracellular space of tissues, where it disrupts normal organ function. This is a fundamental feature of amyloidosis.

 

2. Apple green birefringence is seen with Congo red under polarized microscopy: Amyloid deposits show a characteristic apple-green birefringence when stained with Congo red and viewed under polarized light. This is a diagnostic hallmark of amyloidosis.

 

3. Beta-pleated sheets are seen on X-ray crystallography: The abnormal amyloid fibrils adopt a beta-pleated sheet structure, which can be confirmed by X-ray crystallography. This structural arrangement contributes to the resistance of amyloid fibrils to proteolysis.

 

Other Options:

 

4. AL is a secondary type of amyloidosis: This statement is incorrect. AL amyloidosis, or amyloid light-chain amyloidosis, is a primary form of amyloidosis associated with plasma cell dyscrasias, such as multiple myeloma. Secondary amyloidosis (AA amyloidosis) is caused by chronic inflammatory conditions and involves the deposition of serum amyloid A (SAA) protein.

 

Educational Objective:

questions.stemHtml: Match the following disorders with their genetic abnormalities:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 1-b, 2-d, 3-a, 4-c

 

  1. Trinucleotide repeats → Fragile X syndrome: Fragile X syndrome is caused by the expansion of the CGG trinucleotide repeat in the FMR1 gene. This disorder leads to intellectual disability, particularly in males, and is the most common cause of inherited mental retardation.
  2. Trisomy 18 → Edward syndrome: Trisomy 18, also known as Edward syndrome, occurs when there is an extra copy of chromosome 18. This genetic abnormality leads to severe developmental delays and physical abnormalities. Most affected individuals do not survive beyond infancy.
  3. Trisomy 13 → Patau syndrome: Patau syndrome results from an extra copy of chromosome 13. It is characterized by severe intellectual disability, physical abnormalities like cleft lip, and heart defects. Life expectancy is extremely limited, with many infants not surviving beyond the first year of life.
  4. Hb beta chain Glu → Val → Auto splenectomy: This mutation in the beta-globin gene, where glutamic acid is replaced by valine, leads to sickle cell anemia. The abnormal hemoglobin causes red blood cells to sickle, leading to complications like auto splenectomy, where the spleen essentially becomes non-functional due to repeated infarction and fibrosis.

questions.stem: A patient has presented to the hospital with features of cutaneous vasculitis, synovitis, increased blood pressure, and RBC casts in the urine. He has a history of hepatitis C infection a few weeks ago. Which of the following is the likely lesion seen in his renal biopsy?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Membranoproliferative glomerulopathy

 

The patient's presentation of cutaneous vasculitis, synovitis, hypertension, and RBC casts in the urine strongly suggests glomerulonephritis. Coupled with the history of hepatitis C infection, this points toward membranoproliferative glomerulopathy (MPGN), which is often associated with hepatitis C and cryoglobulinemia.

 

Membranoproliferative glomerulopathy (MPGN) is characterized by immune complex deposition in the kidneys and is associated with chronic infections, particularly hepatitis C. Patients with MPGN often have cryoglobulinemia, which leads to the systemic symptoms of vasculitis and joint involvement, as seen in this patient.

 

  • RBC casts in the urine suggest glomerular involvement, which is consistent with MPGN.
  • Cryoglobulinemia is a common finding in patients with hepatitis C and is often associated with MPGN.
  • The tram-track appearance on renal biopsy (due to the duplication of the glomerular basement membrane) is a classic finding in MPGN.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Membranous glomerulopathy: This is commonly associated with nephrotic syndrome and tends to cause proteinuria and edema without significant hematuria or vasculitis, making it less likely in this scenario.

 

Option B. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS): FSGS also presents with nephrotic syndrome, and it is more common in cases with heavy proteinuria rather than the mixed nephritic-nephrotic picture suggested by RBC casts.

 

Option D. Acute tubular necrosis (ATN): ATN is associated with acute kidney injury, often due to ischemic or toxic damage, and would not typically present with RBC casts or the systemic findings of vasculitis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In a patient with a history of hepatitis C and features of glomerulonephritis, membranoproliferative glomerulopathy (MPGN) is the most likely diagnosis, especially when associated with cryoglobulinemia.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not properly matched?

options.label: A
options.text: Anaphylaxis on blood transfusion: IgA deficiency

options.label: B
options.text: Decreased B cells and T cells due to adenosine deaminase: SCID

options.label: C
options.text: Defective CD40L and CD40 interaction: class switching defect

options.label: D
options.text: Cardiac defects, absent thymic shadow on X-ray, hypercalcemia: DiGeorge syndrome

questions.answerText: Cardiac defects, absent thymic shadow on X-ray, hypercalcemia: DiGeorge syndrome
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Cardiac defects, absent thymic shadow on X-ray, hypercalcemia: DiGeorge syndrome

 

This option is incorrect because while DiGeorge syndrome does involve cardiac defects and an absent thymic shadow, it is more commonly associated with hypocalcemia due to parathyroid hypoplasia rather than hypercalcemia. Hypocalcemia is a hallmark of DiGeorge syndrome, often leading to tetany or seizures.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Anaphylaxis on blood transfusion → IgA deficiency: This option is correct. Individuals with IgA deficiency can experience anaphylaxis upon receiving blood products that contain IgA. These patients develop antibodies against IgA, leading to severe allergic reactions during transfusions.

 

Option B. Decreased B cells and T cells due to adenosine deaminase → SCID: This is correct. Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID), particularly due to adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency, leads to a significant reduction in both B and T cells, impairing the immune system and resulting in severe immunodeficiency.

 

Option C. Defective CD40L and CD40 interaction → class switching defect: This is correct. A defect in the CD40L-CD40 interaction leads to a class switching defect known as Hyper-IgM syndrome, where affected individuals have impaired ability to switch from producing IgM to other types of immunoglobulins such as IgG or IgA.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • DiGeorge syndrome is characterized by hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia.
  • The other options correctly match the disorders with their respective features.

questions.stem: Organize the given steps of Karyotyping into the accurate sequence. Collect cells by peripheral vein using a heparin syringeCulture in phytohaemoagglutininIncubation at 37°C for 3 daysHarvest with colchicineRoutine staining with Giemsa
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 1, 2, 3, 4, 5

 

The correct sequence for karyotyping involves the following steps:

 

  1. Collect cells by peripheral vein using a heparin syringe: The process begins with drawing blood from the patient, using a syringe containing heparin to prevent clotting.
  2. Culture in phytohaemoagglutinin: The collected cells are cultured in a medium that contains phytohaemoagglutinin, a mitogen that stimulates the lymphocytes to enter the mitotic cycle.
  3. Incubation at 37°C for 3 days: The cells are incubated at 37°C for 3 days, allowing them to grow and multiply.
  4. Harvest with colchicine: After incubation, colchicine is added to the culture to arrest cells in metaphase, where chromosomes are most condensed and visible for karyotyping.
  5. Routine staining with Giemsa: The chromosomes are then stained with Giemsa stain, which allows the identification of chromosome bands and facilitates the analysis of the karyotype.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The correct sequence for karyotyping is collecting cells, culturing them in phytohaemoagglutinin, incubating at 37°C, harvesting with colchicine, and staining with Giemsa.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male, with a smoking history of 20 pack years, presented in OPD with breathlessness and chest pain. Further investigations revealed a lung tumor. On staining, cells are positive for chromogranin. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Small cell carcinoma

 

  • Small cell carcinoma is a type of neuroendocrine tumor of the lung and is strongly associated with smoking. These tumors often stain positive for chromogranin, a marker used to identify neuroendocrine cells. Other markers that are commonly positive in small cell carcinoma include synaptophysin and neuron-specific enolase (NSE). Small cell carcinoma is an aggressive cancer that tends to metastasize early and is often centrally located in the lung.
  • Smoking history is a significant risk factor for small cell carcinoma, and the patient's 20-pack-year history further supports this diagnosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Adenocarcinoma: This is the most common type of lung cancer, particularly in non-smokers, but it is not typically associated with chromogranin positivity. Adenocarcinoma cells are more likely to express markers like TTF-1 and Napsin-A.

 

Option B. Squamous cell carcinoma: This is also linked to smoking and commonly arises centrally in the lung. However, it is typically associated with keratinization and intercellular bridges rather than neuroendocrine markers like chromogranin.

 

Option C. Large cell carcinoma: Large cell carcinoma is a diagnosis of exclusion and does not usually show neuroendocrine differentiation, making chromogranin positivity unlikely. It is typically diagnosed when other more specific histological types are ruled out.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Small cell carcinoma is a neuroendocrine lung tumor that stains positive for chromogranin and is strongly associated with smoking.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a true statement?

options.label: B
options.text: Intrinsic pathway activation is dependent on tissue factor

options.label: C
options.text: Pregnancy is associated with reduced factor XI and XIII levels

options.label: D
options.text: Factor XII deficiency does not cause bleeding

questions.answerText: Intrinsic pathway activation is dependent on tissue factor
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Intrinsic pathway activation is dependent on tissue factor

 

This is false. The intrinsic pathway is activated by factors present in the blood, specifically contact activation involving factor XII, prekallikrein, and high molecular weight kininogen. It is not dependent on tissue factor, which is involved in the extrinsic pathway. Tissue factor activates the extrinsic pathway when it binds to factor VII.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Leiden mutation affects factor V: This is true. The Leiden mutation is a specific genetic mutation in the factor V gene that makes factor V resistant to degradation by activated protein C. This leads to a hypercoagulable state, increasing the risk of venous thromboembolism (e.g., deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism).

 

Option C. Pregnancy is associated with reduced factor XI and XIII levels: This is true. During pregnancy, levels of factor XI and factor XIII decrease, which contributes to the overall hypercoagulable state of pregnancy. This change is likely an adaptation to reduce the risk of postpartum hemorrhage, though it also increases the risk of thrombosis during pregnancy.

 

Option D. Factor XII deficiency does not cause bleeding: This is true. Factor XII deficiency does not typically lead to a bleeding disorder, despite prolonging the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) in laboratory tests. Factor XII plays a role in the intrinsic pathway, but its deficiency is not associated with clinical bleeding, making it an exception among coagulation factor deficiencies.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The statement "Intrinsic pathway activation is dependent on tissue factor" is false because the intrinsic pathway is initiated by contact activation (involving factor XII) rather than tissue factor, which is involved in the extrinsic pathway. All other statements about Factor V Leiden, pregnancy-related changes in coagulation factors, and Factor XII deficiency are true.

questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old man, known to be HIV-positive, visited the hospital due to a persistent fever and difficulty in breathing lasting for two weeks. Imaging studies revealed a dense infiltration in the lower lobe of the lung. Subsequent lung biopsy findings were as follows. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) CMV-associated organizing pneumonia

 

The image provided shows large cells with basophilic intranuclear inclusions, which are characteristic of Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection. This pathology, especially in an immunosuppressed patient, such as someone who is HIV-positive, points to CMV-associated organizing pneumonia. CMV infections are common in individuals with compromised immune systems and can lead to various manifestations, including pneumonitis.

 

  1. CMV histopathology: The classic appearance includes enlarged cells (cytomegaly) with basophilic intranuclear inclusions (owl’s eye appearance) and occasionally cytoplasmic inclusions. This is consistent with the findings in the biopsy image.
  2. Immunosuppression and HIV: In patients with advanced HIV or AIDS, CMV is an opportunistic infection that often involves the lungs, causing pneumonia, particularly in individuals with low CD4 counts.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Small-cell lung cancer: While small-cell lung cancer is associated with a history of smoking and often appears as central tumors, it would not present with the characteristic viral inclusion bodies seen in CMV infections.

 

Option C. Cryptococcal pneumonia: Cryptococcal infections, especially in HIV-positive patients, typically present with yeast forms on histology, which appear as encapsulated organisms stained with special fungal stains. The histological appearance here does not match cryptococcal pneumonia.

 

Option D. Tuberculosis: Tuberculosis would typically show granulomatous inflammation with caseating necrosis. There may be acid-fast bacilli seen on special stains, but the inclusions seen in the image do not fit the typical pathology of tuberculosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The presence of large cells with basophilic intranuclear inclusions in a patient with HIV and immunosuppression, along with respiratory symptoms, is highly suggestive of CMV-associated organizing pneumonia.

questions.stem: Among the following statements, what is true for apoptosis?

options.label: A
options.text: There is enzymatic digestion of cellular contents

options.label: B
options.text: It is associated with adjacent inflammation

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Plasma membrane remains intact

 

Apoptosis is a programmed cell death process that is tightly regulated and typically occurs without triggering inflammation. It is different from necrosis, which involves unregulated cell death and often leads to an inflammatory response.

 

This is true for apoptosis. The plasma membrane remains intact throughout the apoptotic process, and the cellular contents are packaged into apoptotic bodies, preventing leakage of the contents and thereby avoiding inflammation. This is in contrast to necrosis, where the plasma membrane is compromised, leading to the release of cellular contents.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. There is enzymatic digestion of cellular contents: While apoptosis does involve the breakdown of cellular components, this happens in a controlled manner, typically through the activation of caspases, rather than the uncontrolled enzymatic digestion seen in necrosis.

 

Option B. It is associated with adjacent inflammation: Apoptosis is not associated with inflammation. In fact, one of the hallmark features of apoptosis is that it is a "clean" form of cell death, where cell contents are packaged into apoptotic bodies and cleared by macrophages without triggering an inflammatory response. In contrast, necrosis causes inflammation due to the release of intracellular contents.

 

Option C. Karyolysis is present: Karyolysis (the dissolution of the cell nucleus) is a feature of necrosis, not apoptosis. In apoptosis, the nucleus undergoes a more controlled process of pyknosis (nuclear condensation) and karyorrhexis (fragmentation of the nucleus), but karyolysis is not typical.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Apoptosis involves the preservation of the plasma membrane throughout the process, and it does not cause inflammation. In contrast to necrosis, apoptosis is a controlled, non-inflammatory process where cell contents are packaged into apoptotic bodies.

questions.stem: With respect to thromboelastography, which of the following are true statements: R time is dependent on the clotting factorsPlatelet activity determines the maximum amplitude in the graphLY30 represents the 30% lysis of the clot and depends on fibrinolytic activityAlpha angle depends on the rate of fibrin deposition
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 1, 2, and 4

 

1. R time is dependent on the clotting factors: This is true. The R time (reaction time) measures the time it takes for initial clot formation to begin. It reflects the activity of clotting factors. A prolonged R time indicates a deficiency in clotting factors or the presence of anticoagulants.

 

2. Platelet activity determines the maximum amplitude in the graph: This is true. The maximum amplitude (MA) represents the strength of the formed clot and is largely influenced by platelet function. A reduced MA suggests either platelet dysfunction or low platelet count.

 

4. Alpha angle depends on the rate of fibrin deposition:
This is true. The alpha angle reflects the rate at which fibrin is formed and the speed at which the clot strengthens. A reduced alpha angle suggests impaired fibrin formation or fibrinogen deficiency.

 

Other Options:

 

Option 3. LY30 represents the 30% lysis of the clot and depends on fibrinolytic activity: This is false. LY30 refers to the percentage of clot lysis 30 minutes after reaching maximum amplitude. However, LY30 does not indicate a 30% lysis but rather measures the percentage of clot remaining after fibrinolysis occurs. Elevated LY30 values indicate increased fibrinolysis, but the specific 30% lysis statement is misleading.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In thromboelastography (TEG), the R time reflects clotting factor activity, the maximum amplitude is determined by platelet function, and the alpha angle depends on the rate of fibrin deposition. However, the interpretation of LY30 does not involve "30% lysis" but rather the extent of clot lysis over time, making statement 3 inaccurate.

questions.stemHtml: A middle-aged lady had a severe headache with nausea and vomiting for the past 2 days. Her blood pressure was found to be 210/160 mm Hg. Her serum creatinine was 3.8 mg/dL. A renal biopsy showed the lesion affecting her blood vessels as seen in the image. Which of the following underlying diseases is she most likely to have?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Diffuse scleroderma

 

The patient’s presentation is indicative of malignant hypertension due to a hypertensive crisis. The high blood pressure (210/160 mm Hg), acute kidney injury (elevated serum creatinine), and the renal biopsy findings point toward scleroderma renal crisis. This condition is frequently associated with diffuse scleroderma, a subtype of systemic sclerosis.

 

In the image, the renal biopsy shows characteristic onion-skinning of the arterioles, which is a classic finding in scleroderma renal crisis. This condition typically involves arteriolar wall thickening with concentric layers of smooth muscle cells, leading to narrowing of the blood vessels.

 

  • Diffuse scleroderma is commonly associated with severe systemic involvement, including the kidneys, where it can cause scleroderma renal crisis, a life-threatening complication.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hepatitis C: Hepatitis C infection is commonly associated with membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN), but this typically does not cause the severe hypertensive crisis and vascular changes seen in this patient.

 

Option B. Diabetes mellitus: Diabetic nephropathy leads to glomerular damage, including nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions) but does not typically present with acute hypertensive crises or the vascular changes seen in the image.

 

Option D. Urothelial cancer: Urothelial cancer is a malignancy of the urinary tract and bladder, but it does not cause the type of severe hypertension or the renal vascular pathology demonstrated in this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Scleroderma renal crisis is a medical emergency associated with malignant hypertension and onion-skinning of renal arterioles, frequently seen in diffuse scleroderma.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true about proto-oncogenes? KIT has decreased expression in GIST.KRAS mutation is more commonly associated with non-small-cell lung carcinoma.ERBB2 over-expression is associated with breast carcinomas.PDGFR-β has suppressed expression in colorectal cancers.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 2 and 3

 

Proto-oncogenes are normal genes that can become oncogenes due to mutations or increased expression, contributing to the development of cancer.

 

2. KRAS mutation is more commonly associated with non-small-cell lung carcinoma: This is true. KRAS mutations are frequently seen in non-small-cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC), particularly in adenocarcinoma, as well as in other cancers like colorectal cancer and pancreatic cancer.

 

3. ERBB2 over-expression is associated with breast carcinomas: This is true. The ERBB2 gene, also known as HER2, is commonly overexpressed in breast cancer, leading to more aggressive tumor behavior. HER2-positive breast cancers are treated with targeted therapies like trastuzumab.

 

Other Options:

 

Option 1. KIT has decreased expression in GIST: This is false. KIT (CD117) is typically overexpressed and frequently mutated in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST). These mutations lead to constitutive activation of the KIT receptor, promoting tumor growth.

 

Option 4. PDGFR-β has suppressed expression in colorectal cancers: This is false. PDGFR-β (platelet-derived growth factor receptor beta) is involved in cell proliferation, and its activation is often associated with tumor growth in various cancers, including colorectal cancer. It is not commonly suppressed in colorectal cancer.

 

Educational Objective:

 

KRAS mutations are commonly found in non-small-cell lung carcinoma, and ERBB2 (HER2) overexpression is strongly associated with breast carcinomas.

questions.stem: Identify true statements about familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP): Autosomal recessive inheritance with late presentationIf not treated, all cases progress to adenocarcinoma of the colon.KRAS mutations cause familial adenomatous polyposisIt is associated with congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 2 and 4

 

Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is an inherited condition characterized by the development of hundreds to thousands of adenomatous polyps in the colon and rectum, which if left untreated, almost always progresses to colorectal cancer. 

 

2. If not treated, all cases progress to adenocarcinoma of the colon: This is true. If FAP is not treated (typically through colectomy), nearly all individuals with the condition will develop colorectal cancer, often by the third or fourth decade of life.

 

4. It is associated with congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium: This is true. One of the extracolonic manifestations of FAP is congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE), which can be seen in some individuals with FAP.

 

Other Options:

 

Option 1. Autosomal recessive inheritance with late presentation: This is false. FAP is typically inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion due to mutations in the APC gene, not autosomal recessive. There is a rarer form called autosomal recessive familial adenomatous polyposis (MUTYH-associated polyposis), but classical FAP is autosomal dominant.

 

Option 3. KRAS mutations cause familial adenomatous polyposis: This is false. FAP is caused by mutations in the APC gene, not the KRAS gene. KRAS mutations are commonly associated with colorectal cancer progression, but they do not cause FAP.

 

Educational Objective:

 

FAP is an autosomal dominant condition that leads to the development of numerous colonic polyps, with a near-certain risk of progression to colorectal cancer if untreated. It is associated with APC gene mutations and extracolonic manifestations, including CHRPE.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old female presents with excessive bleeding following a minor injury. She has no personal or family history of bleeding disorders. Laboratory testing reveals a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) that does not correct after mixing her plasma with normal plasma. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Acquired factor VIII inhibitor

 

The key finding in this case is a prolonged aPTT that does not correct with a mixing study (mixing the patient's plasma with normal plasma). This indicates the presence of an inhibitor rather than a simple factor deficiency, as a factor deficiency would typically correct with normal plasma.

 

Acquired factor VIII inhibitor is the most likely cause of this presentation. It is a rare condition where the body develops autoantibodies against factor VIII, leading to impaired clotting. This condition often presents later in life with no prior history of bleeding disorders, which matches the patient's presentation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hemophilia A: This is caused by a factor VIII deficiency and is inherited, typically presenting in males due to its X-linked inheritance. This patient has no personal or family history of bleeding disorders, and a mixing study in hemophilia would usually correct the aPTT, which did not happen here.

 

Option B. von Willebrand disease: This is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, caused by a deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor (vWF). While vWF is associated with mild prolongation of aPTT, the mixing study would typically correct in von Willebrand disease, and the patient’s presentation does not suggest a familial history.

 

Option C. Factor IX deficiency: This condition, also known as hemophilia B, presents similarly to hemophilia A, and like hemophilia A, a mixing study would correct the aPTT. Additionally, hemophilia B is X-linked, making it unlikely in this female patient without a family history.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In a patient with prolonged aPTT that does not correct with a mixing study, acquired factor VIII inhibitor should be suspected. This condition involves the development of autoantibodies against factor VIII and typically presents later in life, often without a prior history of bleeding disorders.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is correctly matched about liver tumor?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 1-d, 2-c, 3-a, 4-b

 

  1. Hepatoblastoma → Malignant tumor in children with high AFP levels (d): Hepatoblastoma is a malignant liver tumor that commonly occurs in children and is associated with elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels.
  2. Cavernous hemangioma → Commonest benign tumor in which biopsy is contraindicated (c): Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor, and biopsy is contraindicated due to the risk of bleeding.
  3. Angiosarcoma → Plastic pipe factory worker with vWF as marker (a): Angiosarcoma of the liver is associated with vinyl chloride exposure (commonly found in plastic pipe factory workers) and can express von Willebrand Factor (vWF) as a marker.
  4. Fibrolamellar HCC → Young adult with PRKACA-DNAJB1 oncogene (+) (b): Fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) typically occurs in young adults and is associated with the PRKACA-DNAJB1 oncogenic fusion.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Hepatoblastoma is a malignant tumor in children with high AFP levels.
  • Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor where biopsy is contraindicated.
  • Angiosarcoma is associated with vinyl chloride exposure and expresses vWF.
  • Fibrolamellar HCC is associated with the PRKACA-DNAJB1 oncogene in young adults.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding chromophobe carcinoma of the kidney? It is associated with trisomy 7Arises from distal convoluted tubuleCan be associated with Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndromeMay resemble oncocytoma on histologyAffected patients have good prognosis
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 3, 4, 5

 

Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma is a distinct subtype of renal cell carcinoma that has certain defining features and associations. Let’s review the relevant options:

 

3. Can be associated with Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome: True: Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome is a genetic condition that predisposes individuals to several tumors, including chromophobe renal cell carcinoma. This syndrome is caused by mutations in the FLCN gene.

 

4. May resemble oncocytoma on histology: True: Chromophobe carcinoma can sometimes resemble oncocytoma because both tumors have large, eosinophilic cells with abundant cytoplasm. Distinguishing between the two can be difficult, but chromophobe carcinoma has unique features such as the "plant cell" appearance on histology.

 

5. Affected patients have good prognosis: True: Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma typically has a better prognosis than other types of renal cell carcinoma, such as clear cell carcinoma, due to its less aggressive behavior and lower likelihood of metastasis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option 1. It is associated with trisomy 7: False: Trisomy 7 is more commonly associated with papillary renal cell carcinoma, not chromophobe carcinoma. Therefore, this statement is incorrect in the context of chromophobe renal cell carcinoma.

 

Option 2. Arises from distal convoluted tubule: False: Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma arises from the intercalated cells of the collecting ducts, not the distal convoluted tubule. This is an important distinction, as the origin of the tumor plays a role in its behavior and prognosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma is associated with Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, may resemble oncocytoma on histology, and generally has a good prognosis. However, it is not associated with trisomy 7 or the distal convoluted tubule.

questions.stem: Within minutes following an insect bite, a patient developed laryngeal edema. Which of the following chemical mediators is most likely responsible for this finding?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Histamine

 

Histamine is the most likely mediator responsible for the rapid development of laryngeal edema following an insect bite. Histamine is released from mast cells and basophils in response to allergic reactions (such as insect bites) and is a potent vasodilator. It increases vascular permeability, leading to edema and other symptoms of an allergic reaction. The fact that the reaction occurs within minutes also points to histamine, as its effects are immediate.

 

Histamine is responsible for several classic symptoms of allergic reactions, including:

 

  • Vasodilation, causing redness and warmth.
  • Increased vascular permeability, leading to edema (as seen in this case with laryngeal edema).
  • Itching, hives, and other allergic manifestations.

 

Laryngeal edema is a serious, potentially life-threatening manifestation of an allergic reaction, as it can obstruct the airway.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Nitric oxide: Nitric oxide acts as a vasodilator, but it plays a role in the regulation of vascular tone and inflammatory processes over a longer time period. It is not the primary mediator in acute allergic reactions and does not directly lead to rapid edema.

 

Option B. Prostaglandin E2: Prostaglandin E2 is involved in pain, fever, and inflammation, but it acts more slowly compared to histamine. It does not cause the immediate vasodilation and increased vascular permeability required for the rapid development of edema.

 

Option C. Complement C3b: Complement C3b is part of the complement cascade and plays a role in opsonization and phagocytosis, but it is not directly involved in the rapid allergic response that leads to edema. It primarily helps in marking pathogens for immune destruction.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Histamine is the primary mediator responsible for rapid allergic reactions, such as laryngeal edema following an insect bite. It acts within minutes, causing vasodilation and increased vascular permeability, which leads to the swelling observed in allergic reactions.

questions.stemHtml: A 75-year-old man collapses suddenly after moving to the restroom from his hospital bed. At autopsy, he has the gross pathologic finding shown here. Which of the following conditions is the most likely risk factor for the development of this man's immediate cause of death?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Prolonged immobilization

 

The image shows a large pulmonary embolism (PE) lodged in the pulmonary artery, which is a classic finding in sudden death due to PE. The patient's sudden collapse, especially after moving from the bed, is highly suggestive of a pulmonary embolism.

 

Prolonged immobilization is a well-known risk factor for the development of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), which can lead to a pulmonary embolism. When a person is immobile for long periods (such as after surgery or due to hospitalization), venous stasis can occur in the lower extremities, increasing the risk of thrombus formation. When these thrombi dislodge, they can travel to the lungs and cause a pulmonary embolism, potentially leading to sudden death.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Blunt chest trauma: Blunt chest trauma can cause injury to the lungs or heart but is not typically associated with pulmonary embolism, which is the likely cause of death in this case.

 

Option B. Inhalation of inorganic dusts: Inhalation of dusts (such as in pneumoconioses) can lead to chronic lung diseases like fibrosis or silicosis, but these conditions are unrelated to pulmonary embolism.

 

Option D. Bronchopneumonia: Bronchopneumonia is an infection of the lungs that typically presents with fever, cough, and shortness of breath. It does not cause a sudden collapse like a pulmonary embolism and would not produce the gross findings seen in the image.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The patient most likely died from a pulmonary embolism due to prolonged immobilization in the hospital setting. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) can develop during periods of immobility, and when these clots dislodge and travel to the lungs, they can cause a fatal pulmonary embolism.

questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old man has had back pain for 6 months. He recently developed a cough productive of yellowish sputum. On physical examination, he has no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. His temperature is 37.8°C. A radiograph of the spine reveals several 1 to 2 cm lytic lesions of the vertebral bodies. His serum urea nitrogen is 28 mg/dL and creatinine is 3.0 mg/dL. A sputum culture grows Streptococcus pneumoniae. A bone marrow biopsy is performed, and the marrow smear is shown in the image. Which of the following laboratory test findings is most likely to be present in this man?

options.label: B
options.text: Tear drop cells in peripheral blood

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Hypergammaglobulinemia

 

Key Features Suggesting Multiple Myeloma:

 

  • Lytic bone lesions: These are a hallmark of multiple myeloma and result from osteoclast activation by myeloma cells.
  • Renal dysfunction: Multiple myeloma can lead to renal impairment due to protein deposition in the kidneys (myeloma kidney).
  • Hypergammaglobulinemia: Multiple myeloma leads to overproduction of monoclonal immunoglobulins, causing hypergammaglobulinemia.
  • Recurrent infections: The patient’s pneumonia (caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae) is likely due to reduced functional immunoglobulin levels despite the excess production of ineffective monoclonal antibodies.

 

Bone Marrow Biopsy: The biopsy image shows a proliferation of plasma cells, which is characteristic of multiple myeloma.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Markedly elevated D-dimer: Elevated D-dimer levels are typically associated with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) or thromboembolic events, which are not directly related to this patient’s presentation. This is incorrect in the context of multiple myeloma.

 

Option B. Tear drop cells in peripheral blood: Tear drop cells are seen in myelofibrosis, not multiple myeloma. Myelofibrosis is characterized by fibrosis in the bone marrow, leading to abnormal RBC shapes (tear drop cells).

 

Option C. Decreased leukocyte alkaline phosphatase: This is commonly associated with chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) rather than multiple myeloma. In CML, the leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score is decreased due to the abnormal function of neutrophils, which does not fit this patient's clinical picture.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Multiple myeloma is characterized by lytic bone lesions, renal dysfunction, and hypergammaglobulinemia due to the overproduction of monoclonal immunoglobulins by neoplastic plasma cells.
